meta.audience: The poor of the Zoramites, cast out of their synagogues
meta.location: The hill Onidah, in the land of Antionum

world_behind.title: The mission worked on the poor first
world_behind.text: Verse 2 says success came among the poor class after much labor. The Rameumptom crowd of Alma 31 is the other multitude, and verse 7 has Alma stop speaking to them.

world_behind.title: The exclusion was about clothing
world_behind.text: Verse 2 names the coarseness of their apparel as the reason. Alma 31 had listed the ringlets and bracelets the worshippers wore; the dress code is what kept these people out.

world_behind.title: They built the buildings they are barred from
world_behind.text: Verse 5 has their spokesman say they labored abundantly to build the synagogues with their own hands. The complaint is specific and it is about property as much as worship.

world_behind.title: Onidah is a hill, not a stand
world_behind.text: Verse 4 puts the teaching on open ground. Alma 47 uses the same name for a place of arms. The setting answers the architecture of Alma 31 without argument.

world_behind.title: Alma changes audience mid-sermon
world_behind.text: Verse 7 says he said no more to the other multitude and turned to the ones in front of him. The whole discourse is redirected by one question from one man.

world_behind.title: The chapter has four words found nowhere else in scripture
world_behind.text: Coarseness, delicious, dormant, and discernible all occur once. Alma is reaching for vocabulary the record has never needed before.

world_behind.title: The sermon is unfinished here
world_behind.text: Verse 43 ends on waiting for fruit, and Alma 33 opens with the people asking how to plant the word. The seed discourse runs across two chapters.

words.text: Roughness of texture. The word occurs once in scripture, and it names the reason a congregation was excluded: the weave of their clothes. Mormon gives the cause of the exclusion in one noun and moves on.

The waste skimmed off molten metal. The record uses it twice and the King James Bible eight, where Isaiah says silver has become dross. Mormon says the poor were esteemed as dross by their brethren. The contempt is a judgment about worth, and nothing is said about their conduct.

A trial made to find something out. The record uses the word four times, three of them in this chapter and one in Alma 34 where Amulek picks it up. Alma asks only for a desire to believe, exercised far enough to give the word a place.

Delightful to the taste. The word occurs once in scripture. It is the third thing the swelling seed does: enlarge the soul, enlighten the understanding, and become delicious. Alma reaches for taste to describe the part he cannot argue for.
Sleeping, inactive for a season. The word occurs once in scripture. Alma uses it of faith at the point where knowledge arrives in one thing, which keeps faith alive and idle instead of finished.

Able to be perceived. The word occurs once in scripture. It carries Alma's argument that light is good because it can be seen. That is his answer to his own question about whether the experience is real.

phrases.term: They were poor as to things of the world; and also they were poor in heart
phrases.text: Mormon uses the same adjective twice with two meanings. The second poverty is the one that matters to the sermon, and the verse says the first produced it.

phrases.term: Which we have labored abundantly to build with our own hands
phrases.text: The spokesman's sharpest line. They are barred from a building they made. The grievance is about ownership and labor, and Alma never disputes any part of it.

phrases.term: Do ye suppose that ye cannot worship God save it be in your synagogues only?
phrases.text: Alma's first question back, and it dismantles the premise of the complaint. He follows it in verse 11 with a second: must worship happen only once a week. Alma 31 had shown a people doing exactly that.

phrases.term: It is well that ye are cast out of your synagogues
phrases.text: Alma tells people who have just described an injustice that the injustice was good for them. He does not defend the priests; he says the exclusion produced a lowliness they can now use.

phrases.term: Blessed are they who humble themselves without being compelled to be humble
phrases.text: The distinction the first half of the chapter is built on. Compelled humility is a blessing and chosen humility is a greater one, and Alma grants the first to the people in front of him before naming the second.

phrases.term: If a man knoweth a thing he hath no cause to believe, for he knoweth it
phrases.text: Alma's answer to the demand for a sign. Faith and knowledge are defined as occupying different ground, so a sign would end faith rather than establish it. Korihor had asked for exactly this in Alma 30.

phrases.term: Faith is not to have a perfect knowledge of things
phrases.text: The definition, stated as a limit. Hoping for things not seen which are true keeps two requirements in view: the thing is unseen, and the thing is true. Hebrews 11 makes the same pairing.

phrases.term: He imparteth his word by angels unto men, yea, not only men but women also
phrases.text: Alma stops mid-argument to widen the list. Angels speak to men, to women, and to little children whose words confound the wise. He is speaking to people who have been told they are outside the arrangement.

phrases.term: It beginneth to be delicious to me
phrases.text: The last of three things a good seed does, and the only one that is a matter of taste. Alma has moved from swelling to enlightenment to flavor, and the sequence puts the persuasive part at the end.

phrases.term: Every seed bringeth forth unto its own likeness
phrases.text: The rule that makes the experiment work. What grows tells you what was planted, which means the test is real and the result can be trusted without any outside authority.

phrases.term: Your knowledge is perfect in that thing, and your faith is dormant
phrases.text: Alma is careful to bound the claim. Knowledge is perfect in that one thing and nowhere else, and faith goes to sleep instead of being finished. Verse 36 says not to lay it aside, since the tree still needs nourishing.

verses.label: v. 1–6
verses.title: The poor found
verses.text: Preaching in synagogues, houses, and streets produces success among the poor, who were shut out over the coarseness of their clothes and esteemed as dross. On the hill Onidah a crowd of them comes, and their spokesman asks what they should do when they have no place to worship.

verses.label: v. 7–16
verses.title: Two kinds of humility
verses.text: Alma turns from the other multitude and blesses the lowly in heart. He asks whether worship requires a building or a weekly slot, says the casting out was well because it taught humility, and then names the greater blessing: humbling yourself without being compelled.

verses.label: v. 17–22
verses.title: Signs and faith
verses.text: Many say show us a sign and then we will believe. Alma denies that this is faith, since knowing removes the cause to believe, and defines faith as hoping for unseen things that are true. God asks belief first, on his word.

verses.label: v. 23–27
verses.title: Who receives it
verses.text: The word comes by angels to men, to women, and to children who confound the wise. Alma asks only for a particle of faith, or a desire to believe, worked on far enough to give a place for a portion of the word.

verses.label: v. 28–34
verses.title: The seed
verses.text: Planted and not cast out, a good seed swells, enlarges the soul, enlightens the understanding, and becomes delicious. Every seed brings forth after its kind, so growth proves goodness. Knowledge becomes perfect in that one thing and faith goes dormant.

verses.label: v. 35–39
verses.title: Light, and neglect
verses.text: Light is good because it can be seen. Knowledge is still not complete and faith must not be laid aside. A tree nourished with care takes root and bears; a tree neglected withers when the sun comes, because the ground was barren.

verses.label: v. 40–43
verses.title: The fruit
verses.text: Refusing to nourish means never plucking from the tree of life. Nourishing with faith, diligence, and patience grows a tree springing up to everlasting life, and the fruit is sweet and white and pure above all, enough to fill and end hunger and thirst.

chapter.title: A dress code produced the best congregation in the book
chapter.text: The people shut out for coarse clothing are the ones prepared to hear. Mormon puts the mechanism in verse 3 and Alma names it as a blessing in verse 12.

chapter.title: Alma refuses to make the injustice the subject
chapter.text: The complaint is real and he never disputes it. He answers a question about where to worship by asking whether the building was ever the point.

chapter.title: He grants their blessing and then raises the bar
chapter.text: Compelled humility counts. Chosen humility counts more. The sermon gives the poor real standing and declines to leave them there.

chapter.title: Faith is defined by what it excludes
chapter.text: Not perfect knowledge, not a sign, not a thing already known. Alma builds the definition out of what faith is not able to be, and then gives a test that works inside those limits.

chapter.title: The test is self-administered
chapter.text: Plant, watch, taste. No priest, no building, no authority is needed to run it, which is exactly what these hearers have been denied.

chapter.title: Knowledge is granted in pieces
chapter.text: Perfect in that thing, and nowhere else. Alma repeats the qualification three times, and it is what keeps the experiment repeatable instead of final.

chapter.title: Failure is assigned to the ground
chapter.text: Verse 39 says the seed was good and the fruit desirable, and that the barrenness and the neglect are the reader's. The metaphor puts responsibility where it can be acted on.

chapter.title: The chapter ends before the harvest
chapter.text: Verse 43 has them waiting. Alma 33 begins with the people asking how to plant, and the answer sends them to Zenos and Zenock.

applications.title: Answer the question behind the question
applications.text: They asked where to worship; Alma asked whether the place was ever required. When someone brings you a problem shaped by an assumption, test the assumption out loud before solving the problem.

applications.title: Humble yourself before something does it for you
applications.text: Alma says both count and one counts more. Pick the thing you already know you should change, and change it now rather than after it is forced.

applications.title: Run the experiment
applications.text: Alma asks for a desire to believe, exercised far enough to give the word a place. Take one specific promise, act on it for a set period, and pay attention to what actually happens.

applications.title: Nourish what has already sprouted
applications.text: The tree that failed failed from neglect. Identify something in your life that started growing and has been left alone, and put deliberate care into it this week.

questions.text: Who is kept out of things I am part of, and over what?
What have I helped build that I no longer feel welcome in?
What loss of mine turned out to be well for me?
What am I waiting to be compelled into?
Have I been asking for a sign about something I already have cause to believe?
When did the word last taste like anything to me?
Which part of my ground is barren, and do I know why?

entries.reason: the same instruction, at the end of the discourse

And behold, it will become a tree, springing up in you unto everlasting life. And then may God grant unto you that your burdens may be light, through the joy of his Son. And even all this can ye do if ye will. Amen.
